summary: TDD-Agent is a single-agent loop that first writes executable unit tests for a target function, then implements it, and iteratively revises both code and tests from pytest feedback (max 10 rounds). A prompt-only variant is tested on LiveCodeBench and the full agent on the RepoEval function-completion subset (455 problems, 8 Python repos) with GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-Coder-30B.

claims.claim: Test-first prompting (TDD-prompt) beats reasoning-prompt baselines on LiveCodeBench across three models.
claims.evidence: Table 1: TDD-prompt 70.04/67.86/44.87 vs best baseline 68.48 (ICoT, GPT)/67.46 (CoT, DeepSeek)/42.99 (CoT, Qwen). Margins are 0.4-1.9 points with 10 samples/problem; no CIs or significance tests.

claims.claim: TDD-Agent outperforms retrieval and agent baselines on RepoEval function completion.
claims.evidence: Table 2: TDD-Agent-iter10 78.24/90.77/59.34 vs mini-SWE-agent 61.31/84.18/52.97. Numbers present in body. Single run, no variance.

claims.claim: Both test-first generation and dual-track (code+test) refinement are essential.
claims.evidence: Table 4 ablation: Vanilla 68.35/73.63/52.97; TDD-iter1 69.89/76.48/54.51 (test-first alone adds only ~1.5-2.9 pts); Reflect (no tests) 72.09/81.53/54.06 actually beats Single-track (frozen tests) 70.11/79.56 on GPT and DeepSeek. Most of the gain comes from the iterative loop, and the authors' own tool-equipped Vanilla (68.35 GPT) already exceeds mini-SWE-agent (61.31 GPT), so the Table 2 margin over mini-SWE-agent is largely a harness/tooling effect, not TDD.

claims.claim: Generated tests improve over iterations in pass rate, coverage and mutation score.
claims.evidence: Figure 5 (plotted only, values not tabulated in body); MutPy with 20 mutants per problem; line coverage on ground truth.

claims.claim: Most failures are 'matched failures' where code and self-generated tests agree but repository tests fail; credit-assignment errors are <10% of failures.
claims.evidence: Fig. 6; Appendix C Table 11 (max 8.10%). This is an important negative finding: self-tests converge to a consistent-but-wrong state.

patterns.note: Test-first alone gives small gains (Table 4 iter1 vs Vanilla); iterative refinement with self-written tests helps, but dominant failure mode is self-consistent wrong tests (Fig. 6).
Execution-feedback loop drives most of the improvement (Reflect and iteration curves, Fig. 3, plateau ~iter 6-7).
Uses lightweight lexical tools (grep/find, skeleton viewer, line reader); limitations section says semantic repo access is the bottleneck.
Single agent with retained history, deliberately not multi-agent; competitive with mini-SWE-agent at similar token cost (Table 3).
Reports tokens/calls (Table 3) and recommends a moderate iteration cap given plateau at 6-7 rounds.
Evaluation is on public benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, RepoEval).

methodology.sample: LiveCodeBench (10 samples/problem, subset described in App. B); RepoEval function-completion subset: 455 problems from 8 Python repositories.
methodology.baselines: Prompting: one-shot, CoT, SCoT, Self-Planning, ICoT. Repo-level: In-File, sparse RAG, RepoCoder (original config), mini-SWE-agent (100-call cap). mini-SWE-agent is a reasonable agent baseline but uses a bare bash tool, while TDD-Agent has custom inspection tools; no stronger agents (OpenHands, SWE-agent with tools) compared.
methodology.variance: Unbiased pass@1 over 10 samples on LiveCodeBench; RepoEval results appear to be single runs with no variance or significance tests.
methodology.ablations: Vanilla, Reflect, Single-track, TDD-iter1 (Table 4); iteration curves.
methodology.contamination_controls: LiveCodeBench is designed to be contamination-resistant; RepoEval (2023, public GitHub repos) has no contamination control discussed.

standards.peer_review: None stated (no arXiv comment/journal_ref); anonymous artifact link suggests submission under review.
standards.artifacts: Code at anonymous.4open.science link; prompts in Appendix E; generation parameters in Appendix A.

biases.detail: All experiments Python/pytest; Java/JUnit transfer only asserted in Limitations.
RepoEval numbers are single runs; LiveCodeBench margins of 0.4-1.9 points have no CIs.
Agent baseline (mini-SWE-agent, bash only) is weaker than the authors' own Vanilla tool-equipped variant (68.35 vs 61.31 on GPT), so the headline margin conflates TDD with toolset differences.
RepoEval repos are public and pre-date all three models' training cutoffs; not discussed.
Ablation 'essential' claim not borne out: Reflect without tests beats Single-track on two of three models.

coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating their own method — normal self-evaluation, no vendor interest.

verdict_reason: Reasonable multi-model evaluation with an ablation, but Python-only, single-run repo-level results, and the ablation shows the iterative execution loop, not test-first, carries most of the gain. The most transferable finding is the negative one: self-generated tests and code co-evolve into consistent-but-wrong states.
applicability: For the Java team: the transferable lesson is to keep a held-out oracle (existing JUnit/integration tests, contract tests on schemas) that the agent cannot see or rewrite, because agent-authored tests that the agent may also edit mostly fail by agreeing with buggy code. Letting an agent revise its own tests is risky for the domain where correctness is judged against curated source material. Iteration caps around 6-7 rounds are a reasonable default budget. Nothing here addresses multi-repo work, mixed hosts, or Java build latency (Maven/Gradle loops are far slower than pytest), so expect costs to differ.

conflicts_with.detail: Same batch: 2608.17177 reports spec-first (pre/post-condition) reasoning improves bug detection in Google production code, whereas here test-first-only (TDD-iter1) adds just ~1.5-2.9 points and most gain comes from iteration; both find agent-generated oracles can be confidently wrong.
